art.text: The Rashtrakuta dynasty ruled large parts of the Indian subcontinent between the 6th and 10th centuries. Among its achievements was building the World Heritage site of Ellora in Maharashtra.

By the 7th century CE, most key features of the Hindu temple were set down in theoretical texts on temple architecture and building methods. Three styles were identified: nagara, dravida and vesara. The styles were sometimes mixed and not yet tied to specific regions of India.

The Nagara and Dravidian styles of architecture developed in the early medieval period. This came with the rise of Hindu revivalism and the leading role of Hindu temple architecture across the Indian subcontinent.
Ellora was made after the Gupta period, yet it mainly reflects the monumentality and balance of the Gupta style. Its caves were produced under dynasties in Central India.

Ancient Indian architecture ranges from the Bronze Age to around 800 CE. By then Buddhism in India had greatly declined and Hinduism was predominant. Religious and secular building styles had taken forms, with great regional variation, that they largely keep even after the arrival of Islam and then Europeans.

In Karnataka, the group of 7th- and 8th-century temples at Pattadakal famously mixes forms that were later associated with both north and south India. This shows how the temple styles had not yet settled into separate regional traditions.

The Rashtrakutas built the World Heritage site of Ellora in Maharashtra. Their empire ruled large parts of the subcontinent between the 6th and 10th centuries, and it is noted for its architectural achievements.

The temple at Aihole in Karnataka still includes apsidal chaitya hall-type plans. This links its design to older Buddhist-style halls, even as it belongs to the mixed temple styles of the 7th and 8th centuries.

Among the early North Indian temples that survive after the 5th century Udayagiri Caves in Madhya Pradesh is the Lakshman Brick Temple at Sirpur, dated to 600 to 625 CE. A temple at Rajim from the 7th century is also on the list.

The Mayamata and Manasara shilpa texts are estimated to have been in circulation by the 5th to 7th century. They form a guidebook on the Dravidian style of Vastu Shastra, covering design, construction, sculpture and joinery technique.

Isanasivagurudeva paddhati is a text from the 9th century that describes the art of building in south and central India. It is one of the shilpa texts that guided temple builders alongside older works such as the Mayamata and Manasara.

war.text: In 712 the Umayyad army under Muhammad ibn al-Qasim met the forces of Raja Dahir of Sindh at the Battle of Aror, near the Indus River. It was the last battle Dahir fought, and he was killed there.

By the end of the 10th century, the Ghaznavid ruler Sabuktigin had captured the region between Laghman and Peshawar from the Hindu Shahi ruler Jayapala. This laid the foundation for Ghaznavid dominance over parts of present-day Afghanistan and India.

Peninsular India in the 8th century saw a tripartite power struggle among the Chalukyas, the Pallavas of Kanchipuram, and the Pandyas. Although the Pallavas and Pandyas were enemies, the real fight for political domination was between the Pallava and Chalukya realms.

After besieging Debal, Muhammad ibn al-Qasim was joined by 2,000 cavalry from Persia, bringing his force to 20,000. The Chach Nama puts Dahir's troops at 20,000 to 25,000, while modern historian K. S. Lal says they numbered not less than 50,000.

In 973, Abu Ali Lawik, the king of the Lawik dynasty, marched to invade Ghazni, and Jayapala sent his son to support him. Sabuktigin's forces defeated the combined armies of Lawik and the Hindu Shahis near Charkh, in modern-day Afghanistan, and many of their soldiers were killed or captured. Abu Ali Lawik himself was killed in the battle.

Around 765, the Pandya king Varaguna I sacked the Ay port of Vizhinjam by defeating the Vel chieftain. He took possession of the Ay-Vel country, described as a fertile land with magnificent treasures.
The Chalukya rulers, who held power from 556 to 757 CE, were overthrown by their own subordinates, the Rashtrakutas. The Rashtrakutas then ruled from 753 to 973 CE.

The Alchon Huns' destructive invasions of the 6th century CE brought the Classical period to an end. Under the Hunnic king Mihirakula, over a thousand Buddhist monasteries throughout Gandhara are said to have been destroyed. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, writing in 630 CE, explained that Mihirakula ordered the destruction of Buddhism and the expulsion of monks. He reported that Buddhism had drastically declined and that most of the monasteries were deserted and left in ruins.
At Aror, a fireball struck Raja Dahir's elephant, and the animal carried him off the field. Dahir kept fighting but was killed by an arrow to the neck. His army then suffered high casualties.

Sabuktigin took the throne of Ghazni in 977 and began a series of wars with Indian kingdoms. His most remarkable military achievement was the conquest of the Punjab region, which laid the groundwork for the more renowned invasions of Mahmud of Ghazni.
After the battle, Muhammad ibn al-Qasim sent Raja Dahir's body to Al-Hajjaj and sent his army to besiege the fort of Rewar. Dahir's queen, Rani Bai, committed jauhar to avoid being captured.
The Velvikkudi plates of Nedum Chadayan probably remember the Pandya attack on Vizhinjam as the suppression of the rebellious Ay-Vel. They may also refer to it as the battle of nattukkurumbu.

literature.text: The Siribhoovalaya, written by the Jain monk Kumudendu Muni, contains no letters at all. It is composed entirely in Kannada numerals arranged in a frame of 729 squares, and is said to hold around 600,000 verses, nearly six times as large as the Mahabharata.

During the early medieval period, most Classical Sanskrit literature was produced, though in most cases it cannot be dated to a specific century. Sanskrit remained in active use in the Middle kingdoms of India while newly written vernaculars began to partly replace older literary languages.

The Rashtrakuta rulers of the 8th to 10th century made the Kannada language as important as Sanskrit. Their inscriptions use both languages, and the rulers encouraged literature in both. The earliest existing Kannada literary writings are credited to their court poets and royalty.

Pampa (902 to 975 CE) is one of the most famous writers in the Kannada language and is called Adikavi, meaning 'first poet'. His Vikramarjuna Vijaya, also called the Pampabharatha, is the first Kannada adaptation of the Mahabharata and is still hailed as a classic.

Kannada literature is unusual in having a Ramayana and a Mahabharata based on the Jain tradition as well as versions based on the Brahmanical tradition. Kannada epic poetry mainly consists of Jain religious literature and Lingayat literature.

The doha is a two-line rhymed couplet whose meaning is complete in itself, and it has been used in Indian poetry since the 6th century. Svayambhudeva quoted dohas around 800 CE in his Paumachariu and Harivamshapurana. The saint-poet Gorakhnath (809 to 849) chose the form for his Gorakh-bani.
Asaga wrote the Vardhaman Charitra in 853 CE, an epic in 18 cantos. It was the first Sanskrit biography of Mahavira, the 24th and last tirthankara of Jainism.
Shivakotiacharya's Vaddaradhane, dated to 900 CE, is an early surviving work of Kannada prose. It gives an elaborate description of the life of Bhadrabahu of Shravanabelagola.

Ranna, born in 949 CE, wrote the Gada Yuddha, a bird's eye view of the Mahabharata set on the last day of the battle of Kurukshetra. It tells the story of the epic through a series of flashbacks. Poetry of this period was in the Champu style, poetry interspersed with lyrical prose.

The Kavirajamarga refers to earlier Kannada writers, including King Durvinita of the 6th century and Ravikirti, author of the Aihole record of 636 CE. Because the earliest available Kannada work is a guide to grammar and style, it is thought Kannada literature must have started several centuries earlier.
Some early Kannada works are now considered extinct. They include the Chudamani by Thumbalacharya, dated to 650 CE, and the Gajashtaka by King Shivamara II, dated to 800 CE.

Pushpadanta (959 to 972) of Manyakheta chose the doha format for his epics, including the Mahapurana, Nayakumara-chariu and Uttarapurana. The doha is one of the shortest quantitative metres of Hindi literature.

science.text: During the Golden Age of Islam, Baghdad was the Islamic world's foremost hub of intellectual activity. The Abbasid leaders saw that their people knew little about astronomy, mathematics and medicine, so they turned to India and Persia for advanced knowledge. Possession of Sind gave them a crucial pathway to Indian expertise.
Brahmagupta (598–668) found integral solutions of Pell's equation. He also described gravity as an attractive force, using the Sanskrit term "gurutvākarṣaṇam" for it.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: In India, practical decimal calculations were carried out using zero, which by the 9th century CE was treated like any other number, even in division. The concept of 0 as a true number, and not merely a symbol for separation, is attributed to India. By the 9th century the Hindu–Arabic numeral system was being transmitted from the Middle East to the rest of the world.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: An Indian astronomer-mathematician and diplomat from Sind, Kanaka, visited the court of Caliph Al-Mansur (754–775). Intrigued by Indian astronomy and mathematics, the caliph had Ibrahim al-Fazari and Yaqub ibn Tariq translate Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta and Khandakhadyaka. The translations, named Sindhind and Arkand, introduced Indian numerals to the Islamic world.

The Islamic conquest of Persia in the 640s drove a wedge between the Mediterranean and Indian traditions, but scholarly transfer soon resumed. Greek and Sanskrit works were translated into Arabic during the 8th century. This triggered the flourishing of Abbasid scholarship in Baghdad in the 9th century.

In the 7th century CE, the Buddhist philosophers Dharmakirti and Dignāga were the most important proponents of a Buddhist school of atomism. They considered atoms to be point-sized, durationless, and made of energy. This elaborated on the earlier Vaisheshika school of atomism, whose leading proponent was Kanada.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: The ninth-century scholar al-Khwarizmi, who learned Sanskrit, played a pivotal role in spreading the Indian numeral system around the world. His contemporary al-Kindi wrote four books on Indian numerals.
Mankah, an Indian physician at the court of Harun al-Rashid, translated the Sushruta into Persian. The Sushruta was the classical Gupta-era Sanskrit text on medicine.

Water engineering continued in India in this era. Wells were constructed at Dhank between 550 and 625 CE, and stepped ponds were built at Bhinmal between 850 and 950 CE. Rock-cut step wells in the region dated back to 200 to 400 CE.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Persian astronomical tables influenced by Indian astronomy, known as Zig-I shahriyarr, were translated into Arabic as Zijashshahriyar. This was another route by which Indian astronomical ideas reached the Abbasid world alongside the translations of Brahmagupta's texts.

politics.text: In the early medieval period, there were more than 40 different states on the Indian subcontinent. They hosted a variety of cultures, languages, writing systems, and religions. Historians usually date the start of this era to the break-up of the Gupta Empire in the 6th century.

Between the 8th and 10th centuries, three empires fought a tripartite struggle for the rich resources of the Gangetic Plains. The Rashtrakutas, the Pala dynasty of Bengal and the Pratiharas each annexed the seat of power at Kannauj for short periods.

At their peak, the Rashtrakutas of Manyakheta ruled a vast empire stretching from the Ganges and Yamuna doab in the north to Kanyakumari in the south. They rose to power in South India in 753. Their base was the Kalaburagi region in modern Karnataka.

The Pallavas became a major power under Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I. They dominated the southern Telugu region and northern Tamil region until the end of the 9th century. They were finally defeated by the Chola ruler Aditya I.

The Achalpur clan of the Rashtrakutas began as a feudatory of the Badami Chalukyas. Under Dantidurga, it overthrew the Chalukya king Kirtivarman II. It then built an empire based in the Kalaburagi region of modern Karnataka.

The Pratiharas were instrumental in containing Arab armies to the west of the Indus River. Nagabhata I defeated an Arab army during the Caliphate campaigns in India. Under Nagabhata II, the dynasty became the most powerful in northern India.

Under Mihira Bhoja and his successor Mahendrapala I, the Pratihara dynasty reached its peak. By Mahendrapala's time its territory rivalled that of the Gupta Empire, stretching from the border of Sindh to Bengal. The rulers took the title Maharajadhiraja of Aryavarta, meaning Great King of Kings.

The Rashtrakuta ruler Indra III sacked Kannauj in about 916, in a great raid that weakened the Pratiharas. Although the Pratiharas regained the city, their position kept declining. Their feudatories, including the Paramaras of Malwa and the Chandelas of Bundelkhand, declared independence.

The Chandelas captured the strategic fortress of Gwalior in central India around 950. By the end of the tenth century the Pratihara domains had dwindled to a small state centered on Kannauj. The Pratiharas also lost control of Rajasthan to their feudatories.

The Cholas nearly vanished from the Tamil land after the Kalabhra invasion and the rise of the Pallavas. Some migrated to the Telugu country and ruled as chieftains of the Pallavas from at least 540 CE. Vijayalaya Chola later re-established the dynasty as independent rulers in the ninth century by overthrowing Pallavas and Pandyas.
The Pala Empire of Bengal, from the 8th to 12th centuries, was the last major Buddhist power in India. In the 9th century it briefly controlled most of north India.

The Chola power was proclaimed to the eastern world by Rajendra Chola I's expedition to the Ganges and by naval raids on Srivijaya. Repeated embassies to China also announced it. The Chola fleet represented the zenith of ancient Indian maritime capacity.

The Arab traveller Al-Masudi praised the Rashtrakuta kings for supporting the settlement of Muslim traders in the Konkan region and letting them practise Islam. Mosques were established in port towns there in the early 10th century. He reported that the Saymur district was inhabited by about 10,000 Muslims.

philosophy.text: At the start of the early medieval period, Buddhism was predominant across the Indian subcontinent, and the Pala Empire on the Indo Gangetic Plain sponsored its institutions. One of these was the Buddhist Nalanda mahavihara in modern-day Bihar, a centre of scholarship that brought a divided South Asia onto the global intellectual stage.
Between 400 and 1000 CE Hinduism expanded as the decline of Buddhism in India continued. Buddhism later became effectively extinct in India, though it survived in Nepal and Sri Lanka.

The decline of Buddhism in South India began in the 8th century with the spread of Adi Shankara's Advaita philosophy. This shift took place while the Rashtrakuta Empire ruled large parts of the subcontinent.

The Advaita Vedanta philosophy of Sankara, dated to about the eighth century CE, is presented by neo-Vedanta ideology as the central philosophy of Hinduism. The same ideology folds Buddhist philosophies into Vedanta and treats the Buddha as a member of that tradition, merely trying to reform it from within.
The Pratyabhijña, or recognition, school was a form of non-dual Shaiva tantra. It is associated with Utpaladeva in the 10th century and with Abhinavagupta, who lived from 975 to 1025 CE.

Tantrism originated in the early centuries CE and developed into a fully articulated tradition by the end of the Gupta period. Michaels calls the years from about 320 to 650 CE the Golden Age of Hinduism, lasting until the fall of the Harsha Empire.

Epigraphical and archaeological evidence suggests that the Agama texts were in existence only by about the middle of the 1st millennium CE. The Agamas are Tamil and Sanskrit scriptures covering temple construction, worship of deities, philosophical doctrines and meditative practices.
Abhinavagupta (975 to 1025 CE) and Utpaladeva (10th century) are linked to the Pratyabhijna, or recognition, school. It was a form of non-dual Shaiva tantra, and its name means recognition.

The Nalanda mahavihara in modern-day Bihar was a Buddhist centre of scholarship in the early medieval period. It brought a divided South Asia onto the global intellectual stage. It flourished under the Pala Empire, which sponsored Buddhist institutions.

The Agama traditions include philosophies ranging from Dvaita (duality) to Advaita (non-duality). Scholars note that some passages appear to repudiate the authority of the Vedas, while others assert that their precepts reveal the true spirit of the Vedas.

culture.text: Chess is commonly believed to have originated in northwestern India during the Gupta empire. Its early form in the 6th century was known as chaturanga. The game later travelled west and became chess.

In the early medieval period, more than 40 different states existed on the Indian subcontinent. They hosted a variety of cultures, languages, writing systems and religions. Neighbouring regions such as Afghanistan, Tibet and Southeast Asia were under South Asian influence.

Rashtrakuta rule was tolerant of multiple popular religions, including Jainism, Vaishnavaism and Shaivism. Buddhism also found support in places such as Dambal and Balligavi, although it had declined significantly by then. Its decline in South India began in the 8th century with the spread of Adi Shankara's Advaita philosophy.

Islamic contact with South India began as early as the 7th century, through trade between the Southern kingdoms and Arab lands. By the 10th century, Jumma Masjids existed in the Rashtrakuta empire, and mosques flourished in coastal towns such as Kayalpattanam and Nagore.
Muslim settlers on the southern coasts married local women, and their children were known as Mappilas (Moplahs). They were actively involved in horse trading and manning shipping fleets.

The Kabul Shahi dynasties ruled portions of the Kabul valley and Gandhara. They are generally split into the Buddhist Shahis and the Hindu Shahis, with the change-over thought to have occurred sometime around 870 CE.
